newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Local fighters turn on Afghan Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Local fighters turn on Afghan Taleban.

text.p: Local fighters turned on the purist Islamic Taleban militia near the Bagram air base just north of Kabul on Friday, two weeks after it took the Afghan capital, villagers said.

Fleeing villagers said men from Saray Khoeja, which is on the main road north from Kabul that leads to the Taleban front lines some 90 minutes drive away, had attacked the Taleban just after 9 a.m. (0530 GMT).
More than 30 minutes later, the fighting was still going on, a Reuters photographer reported.

He said the sound of automatic rifles and rocket-propelled grenades filled the air as people, many carrying children, fled the village after the third known attack in two days on the Taleban well south of their front lines facing forces of the ousted government.
Trucks laden with goods for towns further north turned back towards Kabul after the fighting erupted following news of Taleban reversals on the front line.
Witnesses said the Taleban were gathering fighters about 15 km (nine miles) to the south of Saray Khoeja for an apparent counter-attack.

On Thursday, there were two attacks on the Taleban between Bagram air base and the town of Charikar, a 30-minute drive south of the Taleban front-line town of Jabal os-Siraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass, which straddles the strategic Salang Tunnel through the Hindu Kush mountain range.

The Taleban are fighting the forces of ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood in the pass and have been forced to break off their attempt to battle into his Panjsher valley fortress as a result, witnesses said.

They said scores of dead and wounded Taleban had been ferried south from the front line. Taleban forces had been switched from the assault on the Panjsher, which runs northeast of Jabal-os-Saraj, to the Salang front.
Acting Information Minister Amri Khan Mutaqi told reporters on Thursday after returning from Jabal-os-Saraj that Masood's forces had made only a "very minor gain" in the Salang area.
Thursday's attacks were attributed by local people to Masood's guerrillas, but the Taleban were still in control of Bagram.

The attacks sent shivers of fright through Kabul, where the Afghani currency, often a good barometer of the capital's security fears, dropped from 14,000 to the dollar before the Salang fighting started to 17,000 on Thursday.
International aid groups met in the capital to revise emergency evacuation plans. Friday's fighting on the main road north appeared likely to heighten those fears.
